cards.intuition: A scan checks items one after another and needs no index or ordering. A missing target can force it to inspect every item.
cards.formula: worst-case scan = O(n); average successful uniform search ≈ (n+1)/2 comparisons
cards.topic: Time Complexity of Linear Scan vs Binary Search vs Hash Probe

cards.intuition: Each comparison throws away half the remaining sorted array. Only about twenty halvings are needed to shrink one million candidates to one.
cards.topic: Time Complexity of Linear Scan vs Binary Search vs Hash Probe

cards.intuition: A good hash spreads keys among buckets, making the expected bucket small. Collisions can still pile every key into one bucket and destroy the constant-time expectation.
cards.formula: expected lookup O(1); worst case O(n)
cards.topic: Time Complexity of Linear Scan vs Binary Search vs Hash Probe

cards.concept: When is index construction worth paying?
cards.intuition: One lookup may not repay sorting or hashing, but a persistent index amortizes its construction across many queries. Include preprocessing and memory in the cost model.
cards.formula: sorted repeated lookup = O(n log n + q log n); repeated scan = O(qn)
cards.topic: Time Complexity of Linear Scan vs Binary Search vs Hash Probe

cards.intuition: Compare the cursor values, advance the smaller one, and advance both on a match. Because cursors never retreat, no input item needs repeated examination.
cards.formula: time O(m+n); auxiliary space O(1) excluding output
cards.topic: Big-O of Intersecting Two Sorted Lists

cards.intuition: Similar-sized lists favor one sequential merge. When one list is tiny and the other huge, searching the long list for each short-list item can skip most entries.
cards.topic: Big-O of Intersecting Two Sorted Lists

cards.intuition: Start an AND query with the smallest postings list because intersections only shrink. A tiny first result prevents large intermediate candidate sets.
cards.topic: Big-O of Intersecting Two Sorted Lists

cards.intuition: Even perfect skipping cannot avoid handling results the query requires. Emitting k matches takes at least proportional work.
cards.formula: materializing k results costs at least Ω(k)
cards.topic: Big-O of Intersecting Two Sorted Lists

cards.concept: Why sequential memory access is fast
cards.intuition: Hardware fetches blocks, not isolated values. Consecutive items share cache lines, let prefetchers work ahead, and support vectorized comparisons.
cards.formula: sequential time floor ≈ bytes moved / effective bandwidth
cards.topic: Memory Hierarchy: Why Sequential Access Beats Random Access

cards.intuition: Scattered probes repeatedly wait for new cache lines or pages and waste neighboring fetched bytes. Pointer chains also hide the next address from the prefetcher.
cards.formula: random-probe cost ≈ misses × miss latency, reduced by available overlap
cards.topic: Memory Hierarchy: Why Sequential Access Beats Random Access

cards.intuition: Cheap decoding can win when compact values require fewer cache lines, pages, and network bytes. Moving data often costs more than simple arithmetic.
cards.formula: compression wins when bytes saved cost more than decode CPU
cards.topic: Memory Hierarchy: Why Sequential Access Beats Random Access

cards.intuition: Big-O rules out designs that grow badly, but hardware decides among plausible ones. Estimate preprocessing, bytes moved, locality, misses, and reuse before benchmarking.
cards.formula: real cost = algorithmic work + data movement + preprocessing + memory
cards.topic: Memory Hierarchy: Why Sequential Access Beats Random Access
